lesson.title: Answering a Riot with an Organization: The Founding of the NAACP
lesson.summary: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People was founded in 1909 by an interracial group of activists alarmed by ongoing racial violence, including a deadly riot in Springfield, Illinois, the hometown of Abraham Lincoln.
lesson.body:
By the first decade of the twentieth century, the promise of Reconstruction had been badly eroded. Groups like the Ku Klux Klan had used violence and intimidation to help drive Black Southerners out of political life, and by the early 1900s most Southern states had layered on legal barriers such as literacy tests and poll taxes to accomplish the same goal without saying so openly. Racial violence was not confined to the South. In August 1908, a mob in Springfield, Illinois, the burial place of Abraham Lincoln, attacked Black residents and businesses over several days, killing several people and destroying homes, a riot that shocked reformers who had assumed such violence was a distinctly Southern problem.

The Springfield riot became the immediate spark for a new organization. A group of activists, including the journalist and anti-lynching crusader Ida B. Wells-Barnett, the settlement house reformer Mary White Ovington, the socialist writer William English Walling, and Oswald Garrison Villard, grandson of the abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison, issued a public call in early 1909 for a conference on Black civil rights. That effort drew on the foundation of the Niagara Movement, a smaller Black-led civil rights group founded in 1905 by W.E.B. Du Bois and others, which had already been demanding full political and civil equality. Out of the 1909 conference came a new, permanently organized body, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, bringing together white progressive reformers and Black activists in a single organization.

The NAACP reflected the reform instincts of the wider Progressive Era, which favored building formal institutions, using publicity and investigation to expose abuses, and pursuing change through courts and legislatures rather than through separate, informal protest. From its early years the organization pursued a strategy of legal challenges to segregation and disenfranchisement, investigative journalism documenting lynching, and public advocacy, an approach that would shape the next figure central to this story, W.E.B. Du Bois, who became one of its founding leaders and the editor of its magazine, The Crisis.
